title: Uniqueness of an ordinary tensor model for fixed adjunction and Hom representatives
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $Y$ any scheme and $\mathcal A$ its category of native continuous-coefficient module sheaves. Use its unbounded derived category and localization $q:\operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Fix a derived Hom bifunctor $H$ and one fixed system $\mathcal R$ of native row-sign product-total Hom representatives into K-injectives, with maps $\rho_{P,I}:H(qP,qI)\xrightarrow{\sim}q\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{row}}(P,I)$, as in [def-sf-native-weil-closed-models]. Fix a CoefficientClosedStructure $S$ on this $H$ [def-coef-ringed-tensor-hom-model], that is, a monoidal structure whose right tensor by each $L$ is left adjoint to $H(L,-)$ with evaluation natural in $L$, including its entire tensor-Hom adjunction and transpose; neither $S$ nor $\mathcal R$ may vary between the comparisons. Let $T_o(P,Q)=\operatorname{ordinaryTensorTotal}(P,Q)$ be the reversed-curried total, with $(p,q)$ summand $Q^q\otimes P^p$ and differential $d_P+(-1)^p d_Q$. A complex $P$ is NativeOrdinaryKFlat when $T_o(P,N)$ is acyclic for every acyclic $N$.

Suppose $m$ and $m'$ are two families of isomorphisms $qQ\otimes_S qP\xrightarrow{\sim}qT_o(P,Q)$, defined for every NativeOrdinaryKFlat $P$ and every complex $Q$. Assume that both families satisfy NativeAdjunctionNormalization for precisely the fixed $S,\mathcal R$ and the usual underived tensor-Hom adjunction. Explicitly, for K-flat $P,Q$, K-injective $I$, and a chain map $\phi:Q\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{row}}(P,I)$, each family admits a chain map $\psi:T_o(P,Q)\to I$ whose restriction to every $(p,q)$ summand is the unsigned underived uncurrying of $\phi^q$ followed by its product projection at $P^p\to I^{p+q}$, and satisfies
$$m(P,Q);q(\psi)=\operatorname{uncurry}_S\big(q(\phi);\rho_{P,I}^{-1}\big),$$
respectively the same equation with $m'$ in place of $m$. Here $;$ denotes composition in diagrammatic order. Then $m(P,Q)=m'(P,Q)$ whenever both $P$ and $Q$ are NativeOrdinaryKFlat. In particular, for the same fixed $S,\mathcal R$, any witness chosen from NativeOrdinaryTensorModels agrees on such pairs with any explicitly supplied normalized model. No equality is claimed when $Q$ is not K-flat, and no equality is claimed after changing the adjunction or the representative system.

proof.text: Fix NativeOrdinaryKFlat $P,Q$ and put $T=T_o(P,Q)$. The native category is the category of module sheaves over its actual continuous coefficient sheaf on $Y_{\mathrm{proet}}$; use a universe in which this site is small. Apply [prop-pur-kinjective-resolutions-exist] to this ringed site and $T$ to obtain a quasi-isomorphism $j:T\to I$ with $I$ K-injective. This uses no boundedness or finite-type hypothesis.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sf-native-ordinary-chain-currying] to $j$. It gives a chain map $\phi:Q\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{row}}(P,I)$ with $\operatorname{uncurry}(\phi^q;\pi_{q,p})=\iota_{p,q};j^{p+q}$. In particular, this is the exact unsigned component equation in both assumed normalizations.

proof.text:
Apply the two NativeAdjunctionNormalization hypotheses to this same $P,Q,I,\phi$, obtaining $\psi,\psi':T\to I$. For every $p+q=n$, their restrictions along $\iota_{p,q}$ equal the unsigned uncurrying just computed, hence equal $\iota_{p,q};j^n$. The coproduct universal property gives $\psi^n=j^n=\psi'^n$ for every $n$, so $\psi=j=\psi'$. The two normalization equations therefore read
$$m(P,Q);qj=\operatorname{uncurry}_S(q\phi;\rho_{P,I}^{-1})=m'(P,Q);qj.$$
The middle arrow is identical because both $S$ (including its transpose) and $\mathcal R$ are fixed.

proof.text: Since localization inverts the quasi-isomorphism $j$, postcompose the displayed equality with $(qj)^{-1}$ and use associativity and $qj;(qj)^{-1}=1$. This proves equality of the underlying morphisms of $m(P,Q)$ and $m'(P,Q)$, hence equality of isomorphisms (their inverses are determined by their forward maps). Apply this to any two normalized witnesses, including a chosen witness and an explicitly supplied one. Both flatness hypotheses are needed to invoke normalization; the argument compares only the fixed $S,\mathcal R$.
